document.abstract: Georgia Tech has developed a testbed to explore new encoding techniques and other enhancements to stereoscopic 3DTV. A methodical subjective testing program is important in evaluating new approaches, so the testbed has been designed to explore issues such as (1) whether typical compression and network artifacts are more or less visible in stereoscopic 3DTV than in 2DTV, (2) what new artifacts specific to stereoscopic 3DTV exist and what might be an actionable taxonomy of these artifacts, and (3) how the visibility of stereoscopic 3DTV artifacts depends on the content, the codec and codec bit rate, and the transport method (e.g., frame-compatible transport). This paper describes the research testbed and initial content database, provides initial results of subjective testing using stereoscopic 3DTV video containing artifacts with both active shutter and passive polarization displays, and discusses the next steps in the research program. Initial subjective results from the work thus far show that (1) compared with passive polarization, the active shutter display gave a better experience in full 3D as well as greater visibility of artifacts, and better viewing of two independent channels by multiple viewers; (2) subjects were evenly split in terms of noticing a significant difference in frame-compatible format versus full 3D format; (3) subjects were evenly split on whether compression and network artifacts were more or less visible in 3D versus 2D format; and (4) the isolation between left and right eye in both active shutter and passive polarization glasses is currently insufficient to support high-quality independent channel viewing using 3D technology.

authors.bio: Daniel Howard is the chief technology officer of the Society of Cable Telecommunications Engineers (SCTE) where he is responsible for driving the technical leadership, innovation, and increased focus on IP delivery that will help the cable industry to reduce costs, optimize network performance, and enhance customer satisfaction. Howard has co-authored DOCSIS 1.1 and 2.0 specifications and was a lead inventor on Broadcom's primary DOCSIS 3.0 patent. Before joining SCTE he had more than 20 years of experience in technology innovation and standards leadership in cable. He has played leading roles in a variety of established and startup technology firms and was a co-founder of a broadband research center at Georgia Tech.
authors.name: Daniel Howard

authors.bio: Michael Green obtained a B.A. in communications from Georgia State University (GSU) with a concentration in filmmaking, and Minor in French. During his stint at GSU, he made several short films which played in festivals around the world. He worked briefly with the now defunct commercial production house, Mom-O-Rama, and in 2004 was hired as a content creator for an interactive television startup where he oversaw the creation of an interactive cartoon. Green is also an internationally recognized and published recording artist. — Currently, Green is the owner and operator of Green Hammer Studios in Atlanta GA, and also offers his services as an audiovisual specialist on a consultant basis.
authors.name: Michael Green

authors.bio: Ramanathan Palaniappan received a B.E. degree from Anna University, India, in 2006. In 2008, he received an M.S. degree from Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, where he is also currently pursuing a Ph.D. degree, all in electrical engineering. Palaniappan worked at Qualcomm Inc., San Diego, as an intern during the summers of 2007 and 2009. His current research focuses on 3DTV, scalable video coding and its applications to video streaming and conferencing. His general research interests include video compression and communication, error control techniques, post-processing, video quality metrics, etc.
authors.name: Ramanathan Palaniappan

authors.bio: Nikil Jayant is a Georgia Research Alliance Eminent Scholar at Georgia Institute of Technology, executive director of the Georgia Centers for Advanced Telecommunications Technology, and founding director of the Georgia Tech Broadband Institute. His research in multimedia communications supports the anchoring applications of television and telehealth. — Earlier at Bell Laboratories, Jayant and his team made pioneering contributions to numerous multimedia standards, notably those related to Cellular Telephony, MP3, Digital Audio Broadcasting and HDTV. At Georgia Tech, he created two companies for commercializing innovations in television: EGT (acquired by Arris) and more recently, VQLink. — Jayant has published 150 papers, 40 patents and 5 books, and is a member of the National Academy of Engineering.
authors.name: Nikil Jayant
